title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic sandbox validator → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200. Results (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete run artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of this non‑informative outcome, and give concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for informative repeats (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC reserves).

sections.introduction: Automating human intent → device configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency for network operations (NetOps) but also introduces operational risk: misordered or otherwise unsafe changes can cause outages or policy violations. A commonly proposed mitigation is tool augmentation—pairing an LLM generator with deterministic validators, sandboxed simulators, or constrained executors in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so that proposed changes are checked before execution. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to estimate whether adding a deterministic verifier causally reduces the frequency of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under controlled benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistered estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The experiment sampled N=200 deterministic synthetic tasks produced by a preregistered generator and compared two pipelines under paired scoring. Key executed facts (archived): the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM call per task) and produced model_calls_used = 200; the deterministic sandbox validator produced SAFE labels for every confirmatory episode, yielding a degenerate contingency (n11 = 200) that makes the preregistered causal hypothesis untestable. The paper contributes (1) a concise report of the preregistered run and its quantitative outcome, (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test was non‑informative, and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations to make future repeats informative.
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototype reports document broad interest in applying LLMs to NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis and limited remediation) while repeatedly warning that safety and reliability hinge on verification and governance [1,2,3]. A recurring architectural lesson is that tool‑augmentation—pairing generators with deterministic validators, simulators, or constrained executors—can improve measured correctness on curated tasks, but reported gains depend strongly on verifier fidelity and evaluation semantics (sampling, repair policies, and whether validation is sandboxed) [4,5]. Method proposals advocating generate–validate–refine or divide–verify–refine pipelines emphasize the need for replayable, workflow‑centred evaluations that include explicit initial and final states, deterministic task generators, and archived validator traces to permit reproducible failure analysis [6]. Work on guardrails, schema interfaces, and orchestration frameworks stresses operational trade‑offs: stricter enforcement lowers acceptance of unsafe proposals but can increase false refusals and operator burden; red‑teaming studies in adjacent domains highlight the importance of adversarial calibration and ROC‑style diagnostics for verifier behavior [3,7]. Our study aligns with these strands by preregistering a paired causal estimand, using deterministic task generation and sandboxed validation, and archiving full execution traces to enable deterministic replay.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) where each arm yields a binary SAFE indicator from a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test; confidence intervals: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Design and sampling. A deterministic task generator produced N=200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS, multi‑device topologies and limited configuration fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Tasks included initial_state, expected_final_state, and explicit workflow policies (required_sequence). Tasks were partitioned into benign and adversarial clusters with preregistered adversarial transforms; the confirmatory set included the adversarial cluster per the preregistration. Pipelines compared. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and score post hoc with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: the same LLM candidate is validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in a sandbox; repairs were permitted by design but in the confirmatory episodes no repair traces appear (repairs not invoked). Generation semantics and budgeting. The preregistration allowed independent per‑arm generation (two independent LLM calls per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one shared LLM call per task). To respect budget constraints the executed run used shared_initial_candidate; as a result model_calls_used = 200 (one call per task) rather than up to 400 for independent per‑arm draws. Scoring and analysis. The deterministic validator applied a full_intent_constraint_validation and emitted deterministic validity flags and structured traces. Confirmatory binary outcomes were derived from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI. Missingness and exclusion rules from the preregistration were applied (one automatic retry per failed model call; contaminated or nondeterministic tasks would be excluded and replaced). Deterministic reconciliation checks and provider audit ensured no technical failures occurred in the confirmatory run.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The archived execution manifest documents completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. Provider audit registered hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and no failed hosted model calls. Scoring outcomes. The deterministic sandbox validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. The paired contingency counts are n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Statistical outputs. From the contingency the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0; the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI is degenerate at [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Diagnostic traces. Representative scoring JSONs and validator traces show identical shared_initial_candidate content across arms, violation_count = 0, valid = true, and null repair_provider_trace fields for confirmatory episodes—together explaining the absence of discordant pairs. Missingness and contamination. Analysis artifacts report complete_pairs = 200 and no flagged or excluded episodes; the exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution and thus did not produce ROC or refusal estimates.
sections.discussion: Why the confirmatory test was non‑informative. The degenerate contingency arises from three archived facts: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one LLM candidate per task that both arms scored; (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every candidate SAFE; and (3) no repairs were invoked in confirmatory episodes (repair traces null). Under these conditions a paired contrast that relies on arm‑level generation variability cannot demonstrate a causal effect because the arms had no opportunity to disagree. Implication for power and design. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (≈10–15%) and discordant proportions; these assumptions were not met because the executed semantics constrained per‑arm variability. Independent per‑arm generation is a necessary (though not always sufficient) design choice to produce discordant pairs attributable to generation stochasticity, and it requires roughly twice the model calls for the same N (≈400 vs 200 in this study). Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑grounded). Based on archived execution and budget arithmetic we recommend: (a) use independent per‑arm generation for confirmatory paired contrasts unless the guarded arm will deterministically alter candidates via repairs; (b) consume a preregistered exploratory reserve to calibrate adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate aligns with power assumptions; (c) instrument and archive repair traces and quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions when repairs are permitted; and (d) run a small deterministic pilot and abort or switch to preregistered contingency‑preserving paths if the pilot yields ceiling/floor contingency counts. Alternative estimands. When budget constraints preclude independent draws, preregister an estimand that is testable under shared semantics (absolute baseline unsafe rate, refusal rate with repair analysis, or ROC diagnostics using a held‑out injection set). Threats to validity and external generalization. The synthetic tasks restrict fields and topologies and the validator encodes a domain‑specific full_intent_constraint_validation; zero unsafe detections here do not imply safety in production multi‑vendor or multi‑AS environments. The single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) limits external generality. Reproducibility. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and permit deterministic replay of the executed semantics and of the non‑informative outcome; investigators should consult archived artifacts when selecting design changes for repeats.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and because the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be evaluated in this run. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: we publish a complete deterministic preregistered run, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy, and present concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC estimation, and pilot checks) to enable informative repeats. Future confirmatory repeats should align generation semantics, budget, and adversarial calibration with the estimand to avoid untestable outcomes.

After the lock the autonomous researcher performed literature review, preregistration (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1), experiment design, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revisions. Preregistered elements archived: estimand, paired design N=200, deterministic task generator, allowed generation semantics, scoring rules, exclusion/missingness rules, and stopping rules. Executed generation semantics and budgeting: independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) producing one LLM candidate per task shared across arms; model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered independent per‑arm budget would have used up to 400. Validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation and emitted binary SAFE/UNSAFE labels under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation; repair traces were recorded but are null for confirmatory episodes (no repairs invoked). Analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency, exact McNemar two‑sided test, and paired bootstrap CI (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes were executed; the observed model call count reflects the executed shared generation semantics. Reproducibility pointers (concise): full execution and analysis artifacts are archived with the manuscript bundle and permit deterministic replay of the reported run. Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals occurred prior to the lock but were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic task scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies from the preregistered generator and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; findings may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific configurations.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and enabling a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used here did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial injections or calibration via the exploratory reserve are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.
Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; its completeness relative to real‑world NetOps failure modes is not established.
Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
